name: Hormone bloodwork panel (total/free T, SHBG, E2, LH)

lead: A hormone panel measures total testosterone, often free testosterone and SHBG, estradiol and LH. Looksmaxxers order it as a first step to see where their hormones stand before working on muscle, leanness and skin.

Clinicians use these tests to diagnose low testosterone and tell primary from secondary hypogonadism: LH is high in primary and low or normal in secondary. Guidelines cited by Wikipedia say a total testosterone below 300 ng/dL can support a diagnosis, and free or bioavailable testosterone should be checked for totals between 230 and 350 ng/dL.

paras: It is a blood draw, ideally in the morning, ordered through a doctor or a direct-to-consumer lab. People often repeat it after lifestyle or treatment changes to compare results over time.

The test itself is a routine blood draw. The caveats are interpretive: levels vary through the day, assays differ, free testosterone can be estimated or measured by equilibrium dialysis or mass spectrometry, and the free androgen index is considered a poor predictor of it. Interpretation belongs with a clinician.

angle.text: This panel shows where your testosterone, SHBG, estradiol and LH stand, so hormone-focused steps toward muscle, leanness and skin start from real numbers. The tests are standard tools for diagnosing low testosterone.

lead: A hormone bloodwork panel typically includes total testosterone, free or bioavailable testosterone, sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG), estradiol (E2) and luteinizing hormone (LH). Wikipedia describes a blood test as the way low testosterone is identified, with LH checked to find the cause [1].

Guidelines cited there say a total testosterone below 300 ng/dL can support a diagnosis, treatment is often prescribed below 230 ng/dL with symptoms, and free or bioavailable testosterone should be checked for totals between 230 and 350 ng/dL [1].
infobox: Total T, free T, SHBG, E2, LH

paras: Primary hypogonadism usually shows elevated LH or FSH, while secondary hypogonadism shows normal or low levels [1]. Normal total testosterone generally ranges from about 240 to 950 ng/dL, and levels fall roughly 1 to 3 percent per year in men [1]. Testosterone can drop up to 13 percent over the day, so reference ranges are based on morning samples [1].

An Endocrine Society position statement expressed dissatisfaction with most testosterone assays. Accurate free testosterone generally needs equilibrium dialysis or mass spectrometry, and the free androgen index is described as the worst predictor [1]. As of 2018 screening men without symptoms is not recommended [1].

No studies found on the panel as a looksmaxxing practice. A case report describes a man whose declining performance and low libido led to testosterone testing and eventual diagnosis of a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma, illustrating its diagnostic use [2].
